text: Hello, everybody.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: My name is Pedro.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I am a software engineer at Airbyte.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And today we're going to be talking about how we built our agent MCP and our CLI.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And before we go into the nitty gritty of all of that, I wanted to give a bit of context on what we do at Airbyte and how all of this kind of fits into our product.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So Airbyte's been around for a while.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We started as the open source standard for data movement.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Connecting all of your SaaS tools that you might be using, like Zendesk, Stripe, GitHub, et cetera, to your data analytics pipelines.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And now we're using that same expertise and have evolved to being the data and action layer for your AI agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we do that by offering our AI by agent product that has what we call the context store, which connects to all of those tools that I mentioned before and sits in between your agents to provide a search-optimized index of all of your data that is able to be more efficiently queried by your agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You're able to gather information about all of these records and contacts and stuff that you might have in all these tools and join them together in an easy way through our contact store.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so our goal is that we want to make data available and actionable everywhere.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we have a couple of different interfaces by which you can access this context store.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One is our SDK, which is more usable if you are building your own agents and your tools.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Our UI, which is just a quick way that you can use it through our web app.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then what we're going to be focusing on in this talk, which is our MCP and our CLI, which is a way to easily make that available within existing agents like ChatGPT and Claude.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what exactly are we exposing through these interfaces?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Three main things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One is the ability to manage all of the core resources of our product to our organizations, workspaces, and connectors.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so all these interfaces should let you interact with that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Second, super important, is being able to authenticate those third-party services that I mentioned about earlier and do so in a way that's secure and doesn't expose your credentials to the AI agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And third, ask and act.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We want to expose the ability to search across the context store, be able to read and write, take action on all those systems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we want all of our interfaces to be able to span across these three capabilities.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the MCP and the CLI, the way that we've structured things is that they are thin, unified interfaces into our platform, not re-implementations of the platform.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So most of the surface layer of these interfaces are presentational, where you take a command and you call the platform and format the results in some way.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And everything kind of sits on top of our shared platform and APIs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And because we deploy a lot, our platform changes like over 10 times a day, we want to keep these things up to date as we go.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so a big part of this as well is OpenAPI specs as a source of truth for how to connect to our APIs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And a lot of those interfaces are built on top of those specs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: OK, so let's go into these interfaces.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Let's start with the MCP.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so MCPs are really great for users that might not be technical.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And in our case, it's great for those users that just want to plug their data straight into ChatDBT or Claude in an easy way.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the cool thing is they're very nicely packaged.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They're very easy to install.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For example, here's our listing on the ChatGPT app listing, the official store that they have.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we also have an application for the Anthropic one, which we're still pending on, if there's anybody from Anthropic out there that wants to approve us.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But even if you're not on these marketplaces, they are pretty trivial to install for an end user.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You just give it the hosted MCP URL, and you're able to connect pretty quickly.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: OK, so let's look at an example.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is our MCP in action.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Here I'm asking, you know, which connectors do I have available?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it goes through, hey, I have four connectors set up in this workspace.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then I can ask it some questions about my data, like show five paying customers with Zendesk support tickets.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so this right now is looking through all the connectors that we have, searching the context store for that information that I asked it about, and then combining that information across Zendesk and Stripe so that it can come up with an answer for me.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Okay, and there we go.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So it cross-referenced Zendesk and Stripe, and then came back with five of those people that have open support tickets.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Cool.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So let's go into kind of some lessons learned while building this MCP and things that you might want to keep in mind if you're doing something similar.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So one thing that we decided to do after a trial and error is to keep the tool count small.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We, for the execution part of the connector where you're pulling that data, we only expose or really deal with two main tools.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One is to describe the connector to get the schema of how do you query that information.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And two is execute that's able to read, write, and delete records.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The opposite end of the spectrum here would be since we connect to so many different connectors and each of these has different entities, different actions you can take, we could have exposed an MCP tool for each one of these.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But instead what we found is really keeping it narrow, using progressive discovery of all of the capabilities that the connector has available and really limiting the amount of context that you shove into the
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Those tool descriptions really helps with the performance of the MCP server.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Two, OAuth is the way.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this refers to how you authenticate the MCP server itself.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is an example for Anthropic.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You click a button to connect, and that spins up our OAuth flow.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you can sign into Airbyte, accept the privileges, and then you are all set up with all the connectors that you've linked up.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And technically, you can use other authentication mechanisms through MCP, but you're really going to have a hard time if you do like bearer auth or anything like that, because the spec is really heavy on OAuth, and all of the clients, the main ones at least, are really leaning towards the OAuth as a better UX for installing that connector.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So that's an example for the Anthropic custom connector
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Registration, where they have no way of you to put a bearer token or anything.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's just all defaulting to OAuth.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So that is very important.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And two, users actually expect to have long-lived sessions through these MTP servers, unlike a web app where you might be OK with having to sign in again a couple of times.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So users expect to use MCPs more like a mobile app, where they don't really have to think about authenticating.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's just available whenever they want to use it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so that has its own little things to keep in mind as you're implementing OAuth is keeping offline long sessions that are stored separately from the web app and have its own set of life cycles.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Cool.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Elicitation, though, is not the way.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I'll get into what elicitation is, but a big part of the MCP server that I mentioned is you need to be able to connect your tools.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You need to be able to give credentials in a way that's safe.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And to do that, basically, when you ask, how do I connect to HubSpot, we generate a link that you go to.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Which pops up this widget, and you're able to select which entities you want to connect and redirect to HubSpot to go through that OAuth flow.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, technically, MCP has something in the spec that allows you to surface those kinds of URLs and process those inputs called elicitation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's a way that you can request information from the user.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For the longest time, it was only form mode elicitation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Which is not applicable for sensitive data like credentials for an API.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But more recently, this URL mode elicitation became a thing that's very similar to what we're doing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But the problem is support across the MCP clients.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So that's a big theme when working with MCP is that even though there is a spec, the features that are supported across the clients kind of vary quite a bit.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is an example from Claude Desktop where it just is telling me, hey, I don't support URL mode elicitation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I can't do that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we have to go back to doing our own thing and not using the spec for that kind of thing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: OK, let's talk about the CLI a bit.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So MCPs are easy for these non-technical users.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: CLIs are kind of the more technical counterpart, might call it the kind of more powerful in some ways that we'll get into.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is the same example we saw earlier, but this time with the MCP.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Or sorry, with the CLI.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Or we're asking, you know, which connectors do I have available?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's this time loading a skill that tells it about the CLI.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then, you know, using the CLI itself to query things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We got back the connectors, then we asked, you know, show five paying customers that have Zendesk support tickets, same as last time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's able to, this time, use the CLI to query that, create a context store, aggregate that data, and then eventually it should come back with
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A result now.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: OK.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So there's those same five users.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So on the design side for CLIs, I think one important thing to keep in mind is to design those CLIs with agents in mind.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Some of the things that might be helpful for users when you're making a CLI are going to be like blockers for agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we'll get into that a little bit more.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The first design decision here that we made was take JSON in and return JSON out.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For humans, it's very nice to specify a bunch of flags to work with CLIs, but when it comes to these more complicated
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Inputs that you have to build to make these queries.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And agents are really good at working with JSON.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They're able to construct this in a much more direct and less of a guessy way than using those flags.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so on the output,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: JSON also makes it easy to deal with longer responses, be able to leverage one of the key capabilities of CLIs, which is, hey, you have this Unix system with pipes that you can redirect the output to different programs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you can use JQ, for example, to select certain things from the output and trim that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so JSON really unlocks a lot of that capability.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Two, consistency is very much key here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So it should be dead obvious for agents to know how to do something across all of the resources that you're exposing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you have structured your CLI in a way that it's structured where there is a noun and then a verb, for example, connectors list, connectors create, make sure that when you're implementing a workspace CLI commands, they also follow that same format.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So Workspace List is another one that we have.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so it's very critical that agents know the right way to do things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it's easy for them to know the right way to do things without having to read a bunch of documentation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And another interesting fact here is if you see agents making the same mistake over and over, calling the wrong command a bunch of times, consider making that your contract.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Make it dead simple for agents to stumble across the right way to use things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Because that usually means that something is not quite as obvious as it should be in your CLI contract if agents keep making the same kind of mistakes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Three, our skills ship with the CLI tool.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So skills are a must when you're doing CLIs because how else, if you have a CLI installed, is an agent going to know that that CLI even exists in the first place?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So it helps a lot with discovery of your tools that are available.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And they also help with using that tool effectively.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have a skill that gets surfaced.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It has a description that is able to come up whenever you ask anything about connectors.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It knows to bring up that CLI and evoke it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then the way that you structure the skill is also something to think through.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You don't want to put too much into the skill that you're going to bog down the context.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Skills have this
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Ability to be separated out into references where you can have a main skill that points to other files in a skill directory that can expand information about the different commands.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that really helps cut down the amount of context that you're loading in and leverages the progressive discovery ability of these agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Cool.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then another interesting fact for Auth side.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Auth was interesting on the MCP side.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It is interesting in other ways for CLIs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Because we can't assume that a human is going to be present to able to interact with those prompts.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When CLIs are being invoked by agents,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It can't sit there and wait for you to type a prompt into the CLI.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You have to expose things either through flags or, in the case of credentials, environment variables and config files so that things can be set up out of band and you don't have to wait for that whenever you're invoking the CLI.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I would say, aside from auth, that's a general thing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A lot of CLIs that are built for humans, you type a command and it'll wait there, ask you for prompts.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that is not able to be used properly by these agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They'll just kind of get stuck there.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Cool.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So CLIs and MCPs, which one is better?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Well, they both have kind of their own trade-offs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: With MCP, the spec is not uniformly implemented across the board.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's a bunch of limits that these providers decide to implement aside from the spec as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For example, Claude has a two kilobyte limit on server and tool call descriptions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's a limit of how long the tools can run, so it's harder to do
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: More long-running processes through MCP.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And there's other kind of limits that they've introduced there.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then on the CLI, the cool things about MCP, like you could have a hosted MCP server that just is always updated.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's not quite the case with the CLI.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You have to think more about versioning.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's harder to keep packages up to date with all those new features.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And there's no, while the limits can be, well, limiting on the MCP side,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Not having any of those on the CLI across the tools, across the calls of the CLI, can make things go wrong and continually go through loops that
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You know, make the agent spin.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so really, I think both have their place.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I think MCPs are great for those non-technical users, be able to quickly prototype things, build one-off reports, and even leverage that MCP ecosystem to have things talk to each other.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then the CLI is better for those more technical users, more longer running tasks, maybe outputs that are super long and you need to leverage those features that Unix and the pipes give you, where you can redirect output to a file, you can do a tail, do a head on that output.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's where really the CLI starts to shine.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: All right.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That is basically all that I had.
